source: Tobacco flowers release volatiles including E-β-ocimene, Z-3-hexenyl acetate, nonanal, Z-3-hexenyl 2-methyl butyrate, linalool, and Z-3-hexenyl butyrate, and blends of them are attractive to H. assulta females (Sun et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most odorants in the response spectrum of HassOR31/HassORco can be detected in headspace collections from tobacco.
source: Most odorants in the response spectrum of HassOR31/HassORco can be detected in headspace collections from tobacco
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the response spectrum of HassOR31/HassORco with known tobacco volatiles.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is a general plant volatile with a green, fruity, and somewhat buttery aroma.
source: As a general plant volatile and most effective ligand of HassOR31, Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is released by many plant fruits and has a green, fruity, and somewhat buttery aroma
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical properties of Z-3-hexenyl butyrate.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is released by many plant fruits.
source: As a general plant volatile and most effective ligand of HassOR31, Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is released by many plant fruits and has a green, fruity, and somewhat buttery aroma
evidence: This is established knowledge about the occurrence of Z-3-hexenyl butyrate in plants.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is present in the headspace collections of tobacco flowers.
source: It is also present in the headspace collections of tobacco flowers (Sun et al., 2012) and hot pepper fruits (Forero et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is present in the headspace collections of hot pepper fruits.
source: It is also present in the headspace collections of tobacco flowers (Sun et al., 2012) and hot pepper fruits (Forero et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is very likely to be used by females of H. assulta as a signal for choosing oviposition sites rather than a signal for searching host plants.
source: Therefore, Z-3-hexenyl butyrate is very likely to be used by females of H. assulta as a signal for choosing oviposition sites rather than a signal for searching host plants
evidence: This is a speculation based on the behavioral data and the properties of Z-3-hexenyl butyrate.

claim: Antennectomized females still preferred to oviposit on sites treated with hot pepper volatiles, but their oviposition preference index was significantly decreased.
source: The behavioral assay with hot pepper volatiles (a complex cue) showed that antennectomized females still preferred to oviposit on sites treated with hot pepper volatiles, but their oviposition preference index was significantly decreased
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiment data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Antennectomized and normal females both prefer to lay eggs on sites treated with Z-3-hexenyl butyrate but had no significant difference in oviposition preference index.
source: Another behavioral assay with Z-3-hexenyl butyrate showed that antennectomized and normal females both prefer to lay eggs on the sites treated with the ligand for the receptor in the ovipositor but had no significant difference in oviposition preference index
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiment data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Detecting host volatile blends in general oviposition is governed by both antennae and ovipositor.
source: These results suggest that detecting host volatile blends in general oviposition is governed by both antennae and ovipositor but detecting for Z-3-hexenyl butyrate seems to be mainly governed by the ovipositor
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral experiment results.

claim: Detecting Z-3-hexenyl butyrate seems to be mainly governed by the ovipositor.
source: These results suggest that detecting host volatile blends in general oviposition is governed by both antennae and ovipositor but detecting for Z-3-hexenyl butyrate seems to be mainly governed by the ovipositor
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral experiment results.

claim: A gravid female moth takes two steps to find an oviposition site: first, she smells plant volatiles mainly by using antennae to search for a host plant, and second, when she comes near to or lands on the host plant, she integrates information from olfactory sensilla as well as mechanical and contact chemosensory sensilla on the ovipositor to determine precise oviposition sites.
source: We speculate that a gravid female moth takes two steps to find an oviposition site: firstly, she smells the plant volatiles mainly by using antennae to search for a host plant, and secondly when she comes near to or land on the host plant, she integrates the information from olfactory sensilla as well as mechanical and contact chemosensory sensilla on the ovipositor to determine the precise oviposition sites on the host plants
evidence: This is a speculation based on the combined results of the study.

claim: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate and other ligand compounds of HassOR31 are expected to play a major role in the second step of oviposition site selection.
source: Z-3-hexenyl butyrate and other ligand compounds of HassOR31 are expected to play a major role in the second step
evidence: This is a speculation based on the functional and behavioral data.

claim: It is believed that ORs cannot function in the absence of ORco.
source: It is believed that ORs cannot function in the absence of ORco (Sato et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Recent Cryo-EM structure of ORco supports a model in which ORco and OR subunits assemble into a heterotetramer with a central shared ion-conduction pathway.
source: Recent Cryo-EM structure of the insect olfactory receptor ORco supports a model in which ORco and OR subunits assemble into a heterotetramer with a central shared ion-conduction pathway (Butterwick et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Oocytes expressing HassOR31 alone had no response to the tested compounds.
source: To test this idea, we injected HassOR31 cRNA alone into the Xenopus oocytes and found that oocytes expressing HassOR31 alone had no response to the tested compounds
evidence: This claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HassiGluR7 was highly expressed in the ovipositors of H. assulta.
source: In addition to HassOR31, the ionotropic glutamate receptor, HassiGluR7, was also highly expressed in the ovipositors of H. assulta and had a similar tissue expression pattern to HassOR31
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data.

claim: HassiGluR7 had a similar tissue expression pattern to HassOR31.
source: In addition to HassOR31, the ionotropic glutamate receptor, HassiGluR7, was also highly expressed in the ovipositors of H. assulta and had a similar tissue expression pattern to HassOR31
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data.

claim: Co-expression of HassOR31 and HassiGluR7 in Xenopus oocytes resulted in no response to tested odorants.
source: To test if these two receptors function together, we co-expressed HassOR31 and HassiGluR7 in Xenopus oocytes, but no response was detected
evidence: This claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only a few sensilla on the ovipositor responded to Z-3-hexenyl butyrate.
source: In the electrophysiological experiments, we discovered only a few sensilla on the ovipositor that responded to Z-3-hexenyl butyrate, the most effective ligand of HassOR31/HassORco, which explains the low expression of HassORco in the ovipositor
evidence: This claim is supported by single sensillum recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The low number of sensilla responding to Z-3-hexenyl butyrate explains the low expression of HassORco in the ovipositor.
source: In the electrophysiological experiments, we discovered only a few sensilla on the ovipositor that responded to Z-3-hexenyl butyrate, the most effective ligand of HassOR31/HassORco, which explains the low expression of HassORco in the ovipositor
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electrophysiological and expression data.

claim: In addition to cooperating with HassORco and functioning in olfactory sensation, HassOR31 might function in mediating cell responses to endogenous signaling molecules, regulating neural development, or play other non-chemosensory roles.
source: We speculate that in addition to cooperating with HassORco and functioning in olfactory sensation, HassOR31 might function in mediating cell responses to endogenous signaling molecules, regulating neural development, or play other non-chemosensory roles
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the high expression of HassOR31 relative to HassORco.

claim: Some AgORs are abundantly expressed in testes of A. gambiae, but AgORco transcript is present at a very low level.
source: The similar situation is also found in testes of A. gambiae, where some AgORs are abundantly expressed, but AgORco transcript is present at a very low level
evidence: This is a comparison to a similar situation found in previous research.

claim: AgORs and AgORco are localized to the flagella of A. gambiae spermatozoa where Orco-specific agonists, antagonists, and other odorant ligands robustly activate flagella beating in an Orco-dependent process.
source: It is proved that the AgORs and AgORco are localized to the flagella of A. gambiae spermatozoa where Orco-specific agonists, antagonists, and other odorant ligands robustly activate flagella beating in an Orco-dependent process (Pitts et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Many ORs are present in tissues outside the olfactory system in mammals and have diverse functions in several physiological contexts beyond odor recognition.
source: Studies on mammals have found that many ORs are present in tissues outside the olfactory system and have diverse functions in several physiological contexts beyond odor recognition (Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A human testicular OR, hOR17-4, was found to control cellular motility and chemotaxis in sperm cells.
source: For example, a human testicular OR, hOR17-4 was found to control cellular motility and chemotaxis in sperm cells (Spehr et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HassGR9 is the ortholog of fructose receptor HarmGR4.
source: The expression of HassGR9, the ortholog of fructose receptor HarmGR4 (Jiang et al., 2015), suggests that sugar taste sensilla are also present in the ovipositor of H. assulta
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The expression of HassGR9 suggests that sugar taste sensilla are present in the ovipositor of H. assulta.
source: The expression of HassGR9, the ortholog of fructose receptor HarmGR4 (Jiang et al., 2015), suggests that sugar taste sensilla are also present in the ovipositor of H. assulta
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of HassGR9 and its known function.

claim: Sugar taste sensilla have been found on the ovipositor of cotton leaf worm Spodoptera littoralis.
source: Sugar taste sensilla have also been found on the ovipositor of cotton leaf worm Spodoptera littoralis (Seada et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The co-receptors of IR families (HassIR8a, HassIR25a) were expressed in the ovipositor.
source: The co-receptors of IR families (HassIR8a, HassIR25a) were also expressed, indicating that IRs may also play chemosensory roles in the ovipositor
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data.

claim: The expression of IR co-receptors indicates that IRs may play chemosensory roles in the ovipositor.
source: The co-receptors of IR families (HassIR8a, HassIR25a) were also expressed, indicating that IRs may also play chemosensory roles in the ovipositor
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of IR co-receptors.

claim: There is no evidence in the literature of any ionotropic glutamate receptor other than antennal IRs involved in the chemical sensation of insects.
source: There is no evidence in the literature of any ionotropic glutamate receptor other than antennal IRs involved in the chemical sensation of insects
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Various types of sensilla including mechanical, contact chemosensory, and putative olfactory sensilla are distributed on the ovipositor of lepidopteran insects.
source: Previous morphology and electrophysiology studies shown that there were various types of sensilla including mechanical, contact chemosensory, and putative olfactory sensilla distributed on the ovipositor of lepidopteran insects (Faucheux, 1991; Klijnstra and Roessingh, 1986; Maher and Thiery, 2004; Seada et al., 2016; Waladde, 1983; Yamaoka et al., 1971)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two types of chemosensory sensilla on H. assulta ovipositors have shapes similar to trichoid and basiconic sensilla on the antenna.
source: On H. assulta ovipositors we identified two types of chemosensory sensilla with shapes similar to the trichoid and basiconic sensilla on the antenna, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4.

claim: The multiporous sensilla on the ovipositor have a large terminal pore, which is characteristic of contact chemosensory sensilla.
source: However, unlike traditional olfactory sensilla, these multiporous sensilla also have a large terminal pore, which is characteristic of contact chemosensory sensilla
evidence: This is an observation from scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 4.

claim: The two types of sensilla on the ovipositor may perform both olfactory and taste functions.
source: Therefore, we infer that these two types of sensilla may perform both olfactory and taste functions
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological characteristics observed in SEM images.

claim: Some sensilla on the ovipositor responded to tested odorants though their firing frequency was lower than that on the antennae.
source: The electrophysiological results indicated that some sensilla on the ovipositor responded to the tested odorants though their firing frequency was lower than that on the antennae
evidence: This claim is supported by single sensillum recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A 100-microgram equivalent of the tested compound stimulated around 20 spikes per second in ovipositor sensilla.
source: A 100-microgram equivalent of the tested compound stimulated around 20 spikes per second
evidence: This claim is supported by single sensillum recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The putative olfactory sensilla identified in the ovipositor of M. sexta have similar characteristics to those in H. assulta.
source: The putative olfactory sensilla identified in the ovipositor of M. sexta have similar characteristics (Klinner et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: This was the first study to functionally characterize an OR expressed in H. assulta ovipositors.
source: In summary, this was the first study to functionally characterize an OR, HassOR31, expressed in H. assulta ovipositors
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main contribution of the study.

claim: Sensilla related to the ovipositor OR have a supplemental function to antennal olfactory sensilla.
source: We also characterized sensilla related to the ovipositor OR with a supplemental function to antennal olfactory sensilla
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: These sensilla were involved in detecting GLV and terpenoid compounds in host plants.
source: These sensilla were involved in detecting GLV and terpenoid compounds in host plants, and most likely played a role in oviposition site selection of this oligophagous herbivore
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: The ovipositor sensilla most likely played a role in oviposition site selection of H. assulta.
source: These sensilla were involved in detecting GLV and terpenoid compounds in host plants, and most likely played a role in oviposition site selection of this oligophagous herbivore
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: Future research should focus on knocking out HassOR31 or destroying the related sensilla in the ovipositor and then measuring how insect behaviors are affected.
source: Future researches should focus on knocking out HassOR31 or destroying the related sensilla in the ovipositor and then measuring how insect behaviors are affected
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research directions.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing method provides a good opportunity to knock out HassOR31 to verify its function.
source: The CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing method provides a good opportunity for us to knock out HassOR31 to verify its function
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research approaches.

claim: The pathway of OSN-expressed HassOR31/HassORco projecting into the terminal abdominal ganglion requires further investigation.
source: Moreover, the pathway of OSN-expressed HassOR31/HassORco projecting into the terminal abdominal ganglion and the function of superfluous HassOR31 in the ovipositor also require further investigation
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research directions.

claim: The function of superfluous HassOR31 in the ovipositor requires further investigation.
source: Moreover, the pathway of OSN-expressed HassOR31/HassORco projecting into the terminal abdominal ganglion and the function of superfluous HassOR31 in the ovipositor also require further investigation
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research directions.

claim: The EC50 value for Z-3-hexenyl butyrate in Xenopus oocytes expressing HassOR31/HassORco was 1.606 × 10–5 M.
source: The EC50 value for Z-3-hexenyl butyrate was 1.606 × 10–5 M
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The EC50 value for Z-3-hexenyl butyrate in single sensillum recordings was 86.50 μg.
source: SSR dose responses of putative chemosensory sensilla to Z-3-hexenyl butyrate (n = 5), EC50 = 86.50 μg
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5C.
